title: Inception
synopsis: You're a thief who steals secrets from dreams. Tonight's job: plant an idea instead. Your wife is dead. Or she's downstairs.

nodes.text: Saito does not want his rival's secrets. He wants the son to dismantle his father's company himself, and to believe the thought was his own. The trade calls that inception and mostly calls it impossible. What he offers in exchange is one phone call to a man in the federal system who can make a murder charge stop existing. Your children are seven and three, and they are photographs.

choices.consequence: You say yes before he has finished describing the risk, which tells him precisely what you are worth and precisely what you will accept.
You make him state the terms out loud in front of witnesses, and he does it easily, which should have warned you how badly he wanted this.

nodes.text: Arthur handles research and timings and disapproves of nearly everything. Eames forges people from the inside out: posture, cologne, the way a man holds a lighter. Yusuf keeps a compound that runs the inner ear ten times deep and leaves the balance intact. What you do not have is somebody who can build rooms that do not exist, because you can no longer build them yourself.

choices.consequence: You go back to a Paris lecture hall and ask an old man for his best student, and the old man asks what happened to your hands.
You consider the architect who sold you out in Mombasa and put the thought down, because Saito already owns him and he no longer draws straight lines.

nodes.text: You give her two minutes, a felt-tip, and a maze that cannot be solved with a straight line. Then you take her under. She lifts a boulevard off its foundations and folds it over your heads until you are walking on the underside of a street with the traffic upside down above you. Your projections turn, all of them at once, and start looking for her.

choices.consequence: You bring her in the same afternoon knowing she is not ready and that you are not either, and knowing that nobody better is coming.
You send her home to think it over and she is at the workshop before you the next morning, because you knew exactly what you were offering her.

nodes.text: The shop smells of chemist's alcohol and cardamom. Downstairs, on cots, twenty men lie under the compound with drips taped into their arms, and the old man who runs the room says they come here to be woken, not to sleep. Down there is where they feel real now. Up here is the dream they endure between visits. He says it without pity, as a fact about his customers.

choices.consequence: You ask the old man your question and he gives you an answer about where reality has relocated for these men, and you dislike how much sense it makes.
You take the sedative, pay in cash, and do not look at the cots on your way out, because you have a schedule and cannot afford the mirror.

nodes.text: He puts himself on the flight and into the seat and takes the line in his own arm, because the man paying wants to watch where the money goes. It also means that if he dies under sedation at this depth he will not simply wake. He knows that. He signs nothing and buys the airline instead, so that nobody interrupts the ten hours.

choices.consequence: You let the client into the operating theatre, and you will pay for that particular courtesy with fifty subjective years on a shoreline.
You tell him a passenger is a liability, and he observes, mildly, that the aircraft belongs to him now, and takes his seat.

nodes.text: She comes through the walls of jobs she was never briefed on. She is not a ghost. She is the part of you that could not put the last version of her down, running loose in the same space as the work, armed and unsupervised. In the Paris test she slides a knife into your new architect's stomach, just to see how new she is.

choices.consequence: You admit that the woman in the rooms is your own construction and that she is getting stronger, and saying it aloud finally gives her a witness.
You call it a projection glitch and move the briefing along, and the girl who nearly bled out under a bridge notices exactly what you just did.

nodes.text: Three levels, nested: rain and a van in a city, a hotel with a bar, a fortress in snow. Time multiplies at each step down, so ten hours upstairs runs a week, then six months, then something you stop measuring. A kick has to land on all three simultaneously or the sleepers below stay under. Yusuf's compound removes the inner ear's vote entirely.

choices.consequence: You sign off on a structure with no margin whatsoever, because the flight is ten hours and there is no version of this that has a margin.
You hand Arthur the synchronisation problem and he goes away angry and comes back with an elevator, a length of cable, and a piece of music.

nodes.text: The mark is twenty-eight, in mourning, flying his father's body home from Sydney. First class, upper deck, ten hours and forty minutes, no scheduled stops. Eames lifts his passport in the terminal so that he has to queue at the desk. Saito owns the airline now, so the cabin crew belong to you and the seat beside him is empty.

choices.consequence: You take the seat across the aisle and offer him a drink carrying Yusuf's compound, and he thanks you, and that is the last honest exchange between you.
You watch him from four rows back and let Eames make the approach, and by the time you meet him properly you are already inside his head.

nodes.text: Level one, and it is raining, because Yusuf drank too much water before going under, which is the kind of detail that kills people. The mark's subconscious has been militarised. Somebody trained him against extraction, so the projections are not pedestrians, they are shooters with a plan. Saito takes a round through the chest in the first ninety seconds and cannot die out of it.

choices.consequence: You put the van through a market and two barricades with the team firing out of the back, and the freight train arrives because somebody put it there.
You drive careful and controlled and lose four minutes you cannot spare, and four minutes on level one is most of a day downstairs.

nodes.text: The van goes off the bridge above you, so the hotel loses its gravity while you are still working in it. Arthur is in a corridor with an armed projection and no floor, dragging four sleeping bodies roped together like laundry, trying to get all of them into an elevator so that the drop registers as a kick somewhere they can feel it.

choices.consequence: You leave the physics to the man who solves physics and go down a level, and he improvises the entire rig out of a cable and a mini-bar.
You spend two minutes of hotel time briefing him on a situation he is already standing inside, and he lets you finish, which is a kindness.

nodes.text: Level three is a hospital built into a mountain and dressed as a military installation, because the mark's own head decided that is what a vault should look like. Snowmobiles, tracer fire, a countdown of five minutes upstairs that runs an hour down here. Eames is wearing another man's face and voice. There is a charge on a wall and a stopwatch in a glove.

choices.consequence: You go up the ramp straight into the guns with Eames laying smoke, and the mark's projections put two rounds through your shoulder before the door.
You take the service route through the ventilation with the clock running, and arrive quieter, later, and with the timing already spoiled.

nodes.text: She shoots the mark in the chest at the door of the room you spent a week building for him. Sedated this deep, he does not wake. He drops into raw unstructured space where a minute up here is decades. Your architect volunteers. You say the word limbo out loud, and everybody in the snow turns to look at you, because you are the only one who has lived there.

choices.consequence: You go down after a man you were hired to burgle, into the place that took your wife, with three separate clocks running above your head.
You let the twenty-four-year-old take the drop and then follow her anyway, and both of you knew from the start you were going down there.

nodes.text: You and Mal built this out of memory and then lived inside it for fifty years while your bodies lay on a floor upstairs. The buildings are all the ones you loved: her father's apartment block, the bridge, the house with the wrong-coloured door. Nothing here contains anybody. She kept the whole city and left out the people, and she did that on purpose.

choices.consequence: You walk the streets you built together, block by block, and every corner produces a version of her that you preferred to the real one.
You go straight for the house and refuse the tour, because the city is a trap assembled out of things you would rather look at than leave.

nodes.text: She is at the table with the plates set out and the children's voices in the garden, and she will not let you see their faces. Stay, she says, and it is not madness. Fifty years down here is a life, and this is the only place where either version of your family still exists. She has been waiting in this house since the train.

choices.consequence: You say no while looking at the back of your daughter's head in the garden, and that word costs more than everything else you do tonight.
You sit down at her table for a moment and pick up a fork, and the moment lasts long enough that your architect has to say your name twice.

nodes.text: You put the idea in her head yourself. One small thought, set spinning like a top in the corner of her mind so that she would agree to come up with you. It did not stop turning when it should have. It followed her out of the dream and across the years and onto a ledge opposite a hotel window. You have never said this sentence out loud to anybody.

choices.consequence: You tell the truth quietly, without defending yourself, and the shade of her listens to all of it, and something in the house begins coming apart.
You say it flat and hard, that she is a fragment and not enough of her, and it is true, and the way you said it stays with you.

nodes.text: In the vault the mark opens a safe and finds a paper pinwheel his father kept for thirty years, and beside a dying man's bed the last word turns out not to be the one about disappointment he has been carrying since he was a boy. Your team built the room. Eames built the father. But what he takes out of it he assembles himself, which is the only way it holds.

choices.consequence: You leave the room without adding anything and let the idea grow in his own handwriting, which is the entire difference between planting and telling.
You reach for one more detail at the door and Eames catches your sleeve, because a single seam is all it takes for a man to see the joinery.

nodes.text: Music in three places at once. The van hits the water and the river comes in through the windows. The elevator drops on a cut cable and everyone in the hotel comes up off the ceiling. The charges take the mountain out from under the fortress. Four bodies surface through three levels in about twelve seconds. Then somebody counts the seats, and the count is short.

choices.consequence: You come up through every layer on schedule and take the seat and the tray and the cabin lights, and you count the team twice to be sure.
You let yourself go back under to find the man you left down there, and fifty subjective years later you find him old on a beach.

nodes.text: Wheels down at seven in the morning. Your team file past you in the aisle and nobody acknowledges anybody. At the desk the officer takes your passport, looks at his screen four seconds longer than he needs to, then stamps it and welcomes you home. A phone call was made somewhere over the Pacific. Your father-in-law is waiting at arrivals with the car keys.

choices.consequence: You set the totem going on a hotel dresser first and watch it long enough to be reassured, which is a habit rather than an answer.
You leave the top in your pocket through customs and the taxi and the driveway, and the not-checking is either faith or plain exhaustion.

nodes.text: You set it going on the hall table out of habit, and then you hear them in the garden and you do not stay to watch. Behind you the sound of it goes on, changes pitch, does something you cannot interpret from this distance. You have spent years being the man who stands over the table. Today the garden door is open and the voices are outside it.

choices.consequence: You keep walking toward the voices and let the table do whatever it is going to do, and the not-knowing is a thing you choose deliberately.
You glance over your shoulder at the last second and see it still turning, and the doubt goes into your pocket with you for the rest of your life.

nodes.text: They are crouched at the edge of the grass with their backs to you, exactly as they have been in your head for two years, and then somebody says your name and both of them turn round. Their faces are older than the photographs. Your son has lost teeth you did not know about. Neither of them asks where you have been all this time.

choices.consequence: You get down to their height and let them talk over each other about nothing whatsoever, and you do not check the hall table once.
Some part of you is already pricing the next contract while your daughter shows you a beetle, and you can hear yourself doing it.

nodes.text: Four plates, one of them your father-in-law's, and chicken slightly overcooked. The light through the window is doing exactly what light does at this hour and there is nothing impossible about any of it. You could take the top out of your pocket right now and settle the question before the salad. Your daughter is telling a story with her mouth full and it has no ending.

choices.consequence: You leave the totem in your pocket and pass the salt, and choosing this over certainty turns out to be something you can practise daily.
You promise yourself one spin in the morning, alone, just to know, and you go on making that promise every night for a year.
Under the table your thumb finds the shape of the top, and you think about the work, and how good you were at it, and how quiet a house is.

nodes.text: You stay. School runs, burnt toast, the discovery that your son will not be lifted any more. The rig sits in a locker in Van Nuys and the rent gets paid on it, quarterly, for nine years, and then does not. Eventually you teach one seminar a term to graduate students who think you are exaggerating for effect. The top lives in a drawer with the spare keys. Twice a year you take it out and spin it, and it always falls, and you always watch it fall, and you are always faintly ashamed of the watching.

It takes about three years to admit the possibility and another to stop it hurting. Nothing here contradicts it. The children age at the correct rate, the coffee is bitter, your knee gives you trouble in the cold, all of which a good architect would include. So you stop asking the question and start doing the work of the answer. If this is a room somebody built, you intend to live in it properly: birthdays, arguments, the hedge. You never spin the top again, and not because you are certain. Because certainty was never the thing you were missing.

You last four years. Then a woman in Nairobi has a problem only somebody who has been to limbo can solve, and you find you are packing before the call ends. The team reassembles slower and greyer. Ariadne runs it now, and runs it better, and hands you a level to build and a schedule to keep and a note about your margins. You take instructions from a student you recruited out of a lecture hall, and you are surprised how much you like it. You are home for the birthdays. Most of them.
